title: The Dare
part: PART ONE: SIXTY-ONE CHIMNEYS AND ONE TROLL

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: A dare is a gift. Always accept it.*

Skye Tanner did not usually look at Rue. She looked past her, through her, at the sunlit middle of the yard where the Bridge Club sat like a parliament of very confident children. But today Skye’s long fair braid was loose, and her eyes were bright with something that looked like trouble.

"Rue," she said, her voice carrying over the rustling leaves of the chestnut tree. "Come here."

Rue’s heart did a strange flip, rising in her chest like a kite that has suddenly found a draft. She set down her squashed cheese sandwich and walked to the sun. The others fell silent. Cedric Pettibone, in his red waistcoat, leaned forward.

"We are playing a game," Skye said. "A real one. Not the sheep game. The bridge game."

"Cross the old bridge," Cedric added. "At dusk. Touch the middle stone. And come back."

He paused, a sneer twitching at the corner of his mouth. "Everybody’s done it."

Rue looked at the mossy hump of the oldest bridge in the distance. It waited there, silent and green, and she realized that nobody had ever asked her to do anything before.
pages.image: A sunlit schoolyard with a chestnut tree; a tall girl with a loose fair braid and a skinny boy in a red waistcoat stand in the center, looking expectantly at a small freckled girl in a mustard raincoat who approaches from the edge.

pages.text:
Cedric was not finished. He had a way of adding things to a rule that made them heavier, like putting a stone in a pocket.

"The troll takes a toll," he said, his eyes bright with invented terror. "One person’s name. If you give him your name, he keeps it. If you don’t come back, we’ll know."

He looked pleased with himself, as if he had built the bridge himself.

Rue felt the warmth of the sun on her face, but a cold thread was winding around her stomach. Under the chestnut tree, Perrin Fen shook his head. It was a small movement, barely a flick of his oversized wool hat, but Rue saw it. He was looking at Cedric, then at Rue, then at the ground.

She looked at Skye, who was watching her with an intensity that felt dangerous.

"Right then," Rue said. The words came out steady. She had said them a thousand times when she was scared, and they always worked. She turned and walked back to the wall, leaving the group in the sun to wonder what had just happened.
pages.image: A skinny boy in a red waistcoat leans forward with a smug expression, while a small freckled girl in a mustard raincoat stands with her hands in her pockets, looking calm; in the background, a thin boy in an oversized wool hat under a tree shakes his head.

pages.text:
Dusk in Bridgewater was a slow, purple thing. It crept over the roofs and settled on the water. The old bridge stood out against the darkening sky, its humpbacked shape distinct against the four others. The stones were fitted so neatly that the joins looked like a faint smile, amused by the town’s fear.

Rue walked the long way round first, just to look. The lamplighter’s lamp at the far end was unlit, a dark bulb hanging in the air. Below, the River Wend murmured, a low, constant sound that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere.

It was beautiful. That was the trouble. It was so quiet and so old and so lonely that it felt less like a danger and more like a secret. No one had ever said that about the old bridge. They had only ever said *don’t go there*. Rue touched her scarf and began to cross.
pages.image: A humpbacked stone bridge at dusk with purple sky and dark water; a small girl in a mustard raincoat and big rubber boots stands at the start of the bridge, looking toward the dark, unlit lamp post at the far end.

pages.text:
The stones were cool under her boots, but as she reached the middle of the bridge, the temperature changed. The stone beneath her hands was warm. Not warm from the sun, which had set an hour ago, but warm like a loaf of bread fresh from the oven. It radiated a gentle heat that seeped through her gloves.

Rue stopped. Her heart beat against her ribs, a quick, hard drumming. She looked down. The stone was smooth, worn by centuries of feet that were no longer there. She placed her palm flat against it.

From somewhere beneath her feet, from the dark space under the arch, came a sound. It was not a growl, or a roar, or the snap of a branch. It was a sniff. A wet, enormous sniff, followed by a very quiet sob. It was the sound of a creature that was tired, and hurt, and alone.
pages.image: A close-up of a small girl’s hand resting on a smooth, warm stone on a mossy bridge at dusk; the perspective looks down toward the dark arch beneath the bridge where a faint, warm light seems to emanate.

pages.text:
Rue stood in the middle of the bridge. One hand gripped the iron rail. The other rested against her cheek, trembling slightly.

The crying came again. Soft. Broken. It vibrated through the stone under her boots. It was a small sound, the kind that gets lost in a classroom or under a blanket. But the dusk was quiet. In that silence, the sob was loud as a bell ringing in an empty church.

She thought of the town. She thought of the almanac. *Do not ask him questions.* She thought of Gran’s locked drawer. She thought of how nobody ever looked under the arch. She thought of Perrin, eating lunch alone under his hat. She thought of Skye, who was used to being followed.

It was the most sensible thing she had ever done. It was also the most foolish.

Rue let go of the rail.

She walked to the side of the bridge. There, hidden by a tangle of greenery, were mossy steps leading down toward the water. She did not look back at the town. She only looked down. Into the dark. To see who needed help.
pages.image: A small girl in a mustard raincoat and big rubber boots looks down at mossy stone steps leading from the side of a bridge toward a dark riverbank, her hand reaching for the rough stone wall.
